summary: In 2019 an attacker used a server-side request forgery (SSRF) against a misconfigured web application firewall to reach the cloud metadata service, obtained temporary credentials for an over-permissioned role and read data from storage buckets. The case is covered here through Brian Krebs's report of 2 August 2019.

overview.background: Capital One ran a ModSecurity web application firewall on Apache in AWS. The WAF's server role could list and read data buckets.
systems: Web application firewall (ModSecurity, Apache) on AWS
An IAM role with broad permissions
overview.impact: A former Amazon employee was charged with stealing more than 100 million consumer credit applications, per the report.
overview.severity: A major data breach reported in late July 2019.
overview.gaps: This file uses a journalist's report. Capital One's own statement could not be read, and Capital One declined to comment to the reporter.

timeline.e: The WAF is deployed with a misconfiguration.
The attacker uses SSRF to reach the metadata service and obtain credentials.
The attacker lists and reads data from storage buckets.
The activity is discovered and a former Amazon employee is arrested the Monday before 2 August.
Krebs publishes his analysis of the case.
Credentials are rotated and permissions reviewed (general response; the report does not detail it).

rootCause.trigger: A misconfigured WAF relayed attacker requests to the metadata service.
rootCause.underlying: The WAF's role had too many permissions and SSRF is not in the default rules of that WAF.
contributing: Metadata service reachable from the WAF host
Skills gap in cloud security (per the report)

evidence.label: On SSRF risk
evidence.body: SSRF has become the most serious vulnerability facing organizations that use public clouds.
evidence.note: Evan Johnson of Cloudflare, as quoted in Krebs's report.

evidence.label: Amazon's view
evidence.body: a misconfiguration of a web application firewall
evidence.note: Amazon's characterisation as reported by Krebs.

diagnose.step: Check what the web tier's role can access.

correct.step: Restrict the role to needed resources.

correct.why: AWS WAF can detect SSRF per Amazon.

fix.safety: Test SSRF only on systems you own.

troubleshoot.scenario: A public web app can be made to fetch internal URLs. It runs on a VM with a role that can read data buckets.
troubleshoot.question: How do you reduce the risk?
troubleshoot.answer: Block metadata access from the app, require session-based metadata, scope the role down and alert on unusual bucket reads.

remediation.answer: List the exact buckets and actions.
Alert on large reads from unusual roles.

design.prompt: Design a cloud web tier that resists SSRF.
design.answer: Least privilege, metadata hardening, egress controls, WAF rules and detection.
